title: UN votes to adopt new map that makes our world look different
description: The United Nations General Assembly voted on Friday to adopt a new world map that reflects countries’ true relative sizes, after African nations urged the UN to right a centuries-old wrong.
fullText:
The United Nations General Assembly voted on Friday to adopt a new world map that reflects countries’ true relative sizes, after African nations urged the UN to right a centuries-old wrong.

The “Correct the Map” resolution –– put forward by African Union member states, as well as the Bahamas –– passed with overwhelming support: 164 member states voted in favor, six abstained and only the United States voted against it.

The resolution aims to give an “equitable” representation of the globe’s regions, particularly Africa, arguing that the distortions in the current world map mean the continent has undergone a “symbolic minimization” in people’s collective imagination.

At present, many of the world’s maps are based on the Mercator projection, created by European cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569. It is widely used for navigation since the north-south lines have constant true bearings relative to the equator.

However, it is less useful as a world map since the scale is distorted, with countries further from the equator appearing disproportionately larger than those closest. For example, on the Mercator, Greenland appears larger than the continent of South America and appears similar in size to Africa.

In reality, Greenland is roughly the size of the Democratic Republic of Congo and Africa is 14 times the size of Greenland.

Some critics of the Mercator projection suspect it has remained widely used because it enlarges and centers Europe, as well as other Western regions such as North America, perpetuating ideas of European superiority.

The UN resolution notes “with concern that this distortion contributes to minimizing the perceived sizes of Africa, Latin America and South Asia, and perpetuating an unbalanced view of the world.”

It adds that the distortions also “contribute to minimizing the extent of socioeconomic realities, infrastructure needs, development potential and prosperity in the Southern regions, and that they can fuel prejudices in the environmental, geopolitical and security fields.”

The resolution therefore proposes, as an “act of cognitive justice and memorial reparation,” that the Mercator projection is replaced with the Equal Earth projection, which depicts the relative surface areas of the world’s regions more accurately.

In the Equal Earth, which was introduced at the 2018 North American Cartographic Information Society conference, Europe appears to shrink, Brazil balloons, and Greenland dramatically diminishes. Africa appears much larger in comparison.

France’s foreign affairs minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, announced Friday that France “will abandon the Mercator projection” in favor of representations that more accurately depict countries’ surface areas, state-owned TV network France 24 reported.

“The United States, Russia and China take on a disproportionate visual prominence compared to Africa, Latin America or southeast Asia,” Barrot said, adding that “distortions eventually take root in perceptions” and that “the time has come to correct them.”

The UN vote comes after the African Union adopted the Equal Earth Map in March and after Togo, on behalf of the AU, asked UN member states in April to do the same. As a result, a draft resolution was created and the UN General Assembly held informal consultations on it in July.

“Africa, once diminished on maps, now insists on being seen at its true scale – geographically, historically, morally, culturally, economically, diplomatically and globally,” Amma Twum-Amoah, commissioner for the AU’s Department of Health, Humanitarian Affairs and Social Development, said in a statement in March.

New Zealand has also taken issue with the Mercator map, with a tourism ad back in 2018 – featuring then-Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern – joking that “New Zealand is disappearing off the world maps” due to its position in the bottom right-hand corner.

The Equal Earth map addresses this, coming in various forms, including one that centers Oceania, rather than Greenwich, London. Greenwich has long been used as the standard for world time and global geographical reference.

Digital map platforms such as Google Maps also currently use a version of the Mercator projection. The draft resolution urges tech platforms to engage with UN member states and regional organizations and adopt the more accurate projection.

title: South Africa finish strongly to take 2-1 series lead against All Blacks
description: South Africa eventually overpower a spirited New Zealand as the world champions came on strong in the final quarter in Soweto to take a 2-1 series lead.
fullText:
Greatest Rivalry Series - third Test

Tries: Arendse, penalty try, Kriel, Marx Cons: Mngomezulu 2 Pens: Mngomezulu

Tries: Savea 2, Jordan, Taukei'aho Cons: Love, McKenzie

South Africa eventually overpowered a spirited New Zealand, who could only outrun their hosts' set-piece power for so long, as the world champions came on strong in the final quarter in Soweto to take a 2-1 lead in a high-quality 'Greatest Rivalry' series.

The two sides traded two tries each in a tight first half, with New Zealand's composure and ambition with ball in hand stretching South Africa's onrushing defence.

The All Blacks sniffed a famous victory when Will Jordan chased after his own kick ahead and crossed for a 17-12 lead in the 55th minute.

But, shortly after, Jesse Kriel barged through Leroy Carter to cross at the other end and, reprieved, South Africa took full advantage.

Malcolm Marx plunged over at the back of juggernaut maul and a Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu penalty gave South Africa a cushion that Samisoni Taukei'aho's final-play try could dent, but not fully deflate.

The two teams will meet in a fourth and final Test in the American city of Baltimore next weekend, with New Zealand, who won the opening match, looking to snatch a draw in the series.

With Springbok captain Siya Kolisi calling on his team to honour those who died in nearby Soweto during the fight against apartheid, and national pride stung by New Zealand coach Dave Rennie's criticism of their scrum technique, Soccer City was braced for a fast start by the hosts.

New Zealand's smarts initially defused the fire and fury inside the cauldron, however.

After a brave Peter Lakai turnover had halted South Africa momentum, Will Jordan streaked clear to switch play to the other 22.

South Africa fly-half Feinberg-Mngomezulu was shown yellow for knocking down Ardie Savea's offload and, from the resulting penalty, the All Blacks rolled round the back of a short-range line-out, clearing room for Savea to sweep through some under-staffed fringe defence and score.

With Cheslin Kolbe, with a perfect goal-kicking record so far in the series, having departed with a head knock, South Africa had taken a dent to their confidence, as well as the scoreboard.

New Zealand had ducked and dived to minimise the effect of South Africa's set-piece supremacy.

Fast strikes from hooker Asafo Aumua had got the ball away from a fast-retreating scrum, while trick plays and the addition of Lakai as a jumping option kept South Africa from competing successfully at the line-out.

South Africa built momentum regardless though and All Black discipline frayed as Damian de Allende shrugged off Carter and fed Kurt-Lee Arendse to score in the 21st minute after a string of penalty offences from the away side.

New Zealand pulled back 12-5 ahead soon after with the agility and speed of second rows Sam Darry and Tupou Vaa'i buying territory and Savea on hand to scoop up and scoot over following Arendse's tackle on Carter out wide.

It is impossible to keep the South Africa's coshing scrum power out of the game, however.

Rennie had accused South Africa's front row of 'walking around' their opposite numbers in their second Test win in Cape Town last weekend. Marx, Wilco Louw and Ox Nche duly took route one, ploughing through the All Blacks front row to force a penalty try and ensure parity at half-time.

While another Test awaits in the United States, the sense of an unofficial series being on the line was tangible.

New Zealand have won on South African soil only once before, when the Incomparables of 1996 returned with a 2-1 victory.

Fly-half Ruben Love missed a long-range shot at goal after the interval with the stakes suffocatingly high.

Jordan's try, from Carter's pop off the floor, briefly opened up scoreboard space on 55 minutes, but South Africa edged ahead for the first time two minutes later as Kriel shrugged off a soft tackle and scampered in.

The hosts took a 19-17 advantage into the final quarter and, with the All Blacks lacking Savea's leadership after their captain was forced off with a shoulder injury in the first half, the Boks landed a knockout blow in familiar fashion.

Scrum pressure forced New Zealand replacement Fletcher Newell to his knees, the Springboks punted the resulting penalty into the 22m and a monster maul rumbled infield and forward with Marx crashing over.

Feinberg-Mngomezulu added the extras for a 26-17 lead and slotted a 70th-minute penalty to push the lead out to 12 points.

The 85,976-strong crowd went through their celebratory songbook, dusting off their Cranberries-inspired ode to head coach Rassie Erasmus.

Taukei'aho's try was too little, too late to change the tune of the contest, but the rest of the rugby world will take heart from how hard his side have pushed the Springboks in all three of their meetings.

title: Modric plans to play for Croatia past 41st birthday
description: Luke Modric, 41, is not ready to retire from international football and hopes to play for Croatia in upcoming Nations League games, including against England.
fullText:
Luka Modric turns 41 on Wednesday but is not ready to retire from international football just yet.

The Croatia FA has announced, external that their captain intends to continue playing for the national team in upcoming Nations League games, including against England.

His decision coincides with the return of Slaven Bilic as manager, with the former West Ham boss helping to guide Modric's fledgling international career in his first stint in charge of the Croatia side, between 2006 and 2012.

Modric earned his first senior cap in March 2006, just before Bilic was named Croatia manager for the first time, and has since gone on to make 202 appearances for his country.

He was expected to call it a day after this summer's World Cup, when Zlatko Dalic's side were knocked out in the last 32 by Portugal.

"Of course, Luka's decision makes me extremely happy," said Bilic, who was manager of Croatia when they denied Steve McLaren's England side qualification for the 2008 Euros.

"We are all aware what he brings to Croatia, both on and off the pitch.

"I'm looking forward to working with him again, after 14 years, and we both share a strong ambition to keep Croatia a top, successful team, shoulder to shoulder with the best teams in the world."

Modric, who currently plays for AC Milan, won the Golden Ball at the 2018 World Cup in Russia, when he helped Croatia reach the final, where they lost to France.

He was also part of the side that finished third in Qatar, four years later.

After playing his part in McLaren's "wally with the brolly" moment at Wembley in the 2008 Euro qualifiers, Modric helped Croatia reach the quarter-finals in Austria and Switzerland.

Croatia's next internationals are in the in the Nations League - away to Czech Republic on 26 September and Spain on 29 September.

They then host England in the competition on 3 October, with the return fixture at Wembley on 12 November.

title: Taylor v Pili - Irish icon's farewell fight predictions
description: Figures from the boxing world give their predictions for Katie Taylor's farewell fight against Flora Pili in Dublin on Saturday. .
fullText:
Katie Taylor brings the curtain down on a remarkable career on Saturday when she faces unbeaten Flora Pili in front of 80,000 fans at Croke Park in Dublin.

Taylor is an Olympic gold medallist and two-weight undisputed champion who has won 25 of her 26 professional fights, with six victories by stoppage.

The 40-year-old has long dreamed of fighting at Croke Park and will finally get her wish in the final bout of her career.

French challenger Pili, 29, is undefeated in 12 professional contests, with two stoppage wins. She is former European champion, but has never faced anyone with Taylor's pedigree or experience.

Victory in the light-welterweight contest would provide a fairytale ending for one of Ireland's greatest sporting careers and see Taylor become an undisputed champion for a third time.

Can Taylor produce one final vintage performance on the biggest night of her career?

Or will the younger, unbeaten Pili spoil the occasion and pull off a mammoth upset?

BBC Sport spoke to figures from the boxing world to get their predictions for Saturday's fight.

"Saturday is the perfect tribute to probably the greatest female boxer that has ever lived in Katie Taylor. Flora Pili has the perfect style that will make Katie Taylor look great.

"It'll be a brilliant night and it will be capped off with a fantastic performance from Katie Taylor."

"100% Katie Taylor wins. It will be a night where she captures the hearts of not just Ireland but so many nations. She is the purest of souls and that is so much more of boxing. I pray that when she leaves that ring she knows what she has done for the people who will come through in boxing."

"I think we see Katie rolling back the years and one more Katie Taylor performance. I wouldn't be surprised if we saw a late stoppage and capped an unbelievable career. She will get a homecoming fit for a queen.

"I'm very jealous I'm not there but I'm not ruling out getting a flight there and doing an all-nighter and getting the 6am flight back home."

"Katie Taylor is going to have an amazing performance and this is what she's wanted at Croke Park. Taylor will give it her all during her last rodeo and will put on an amazing performance to get the win."

"I've watched bits of Pili and she looks OK, but Katie is on a different level and should win, will win. It will be the icing on the cake for Katie to end a career that we may never see again from a fighter from these shores.

"It's a little harder for the women to get stoppages with the two-minute rounds, but I feel Katie may well find a finish in the later rounds."

title: Former world champion Ruiz Jr loses comeback fight
description: American heavyweight Andy Ruiz Jr, who shocked Anthony Joshua in 2019 to take his world titles, loses comeback fight to Poland's Damian Knyba.
fullText:
Former world champion Andy Ruiz Jr has vowed to carry on after losing his comeback fight to Poland's Damian Knyba in New Jersey.

The 36-year-old heavyweight shocked the boxing world seven years ago by beating Britain's Anthony Joshua to take his world titles.

Ruiz Jr has since been beset by injuries and was taking part in just his fourth fight since losing the rematch to Joshua in December 2019.

He looked a shadow of his former self at the Prudential Center in Newark, saved by the bell after scrambling back to his feet following a knockdown in the seventh, he eventually lost by a unanimous points decision.

Judges scored the fight 117-110, 114-113 and 114-113 in favour of the Pole, who took his record to 18 wins and one defeat, but Ruiz Jr was quick to demand a rematch.

"I don't know, I think it was just him holding," said Ruiz Jr, who recently signed up with British promoter Eddie Hearn.

"Every time I tried to come in, he'd hold me really tight, and I just couldn't let my combinations go.

"He played a good game plan, but I'd love to run it back and do things a lot different."

Joshua's former conqueror argued that he was simply rusty after taking his first fight since drawing with American Jarrell Miller in August 2024.

"It was just a long layoff, and it was a great opponent," he argued.

"I didn't want to take an easy fight, so that's why I took Damian. He's a big guy. But we've got to take risks. I've still got it in me, man. I've just got to stay active and I want to fight again."

fullText:
A spate of serious safety incidents have increased fears about the power and impenetrability of the most advanced models

Picture humanity in a boat being swept down a raging river, praying there is no Niagara Falls ahead. Or imagine standing with the pioneering physicists in 1942 before they triggered the first self-sustaining nuclear fission chain reaction beneath a Chicago stadium.

These were two of the analogies used this week by Prof Robert Trager, an expert in the nascent field of AI governance, to describe the perilous but potential-filled moment the world stands at with accelerating artificial intelligence.

Trager, the director of the Oxford Martin AI Governance Initiative, was speaking in the week OpenAI claimed the technology had crossed the threshold known as AGI – artificial general intelligence – with its newest model, GPT-6 Astra.

That claim came as the company prepared for a potential $850bn (£630bn) stock flotation, so included a dose of marketing spin, but if true it may be significant. The San Francisco company defines AGI as “autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work”.

The tasks it claims Astra can automate include designing circuit boards, filling out tax returns, building video games, financial modelling, engineering design and helping assemble legal documents. The threat to some white-collar jobs is implicit.

Yet, the AGI claim coincides with rising fears about AI risks among safety experts and political leaders, whose nerves have been jangled by the increasing power and impenetrability of AI models this summer and a spate of serious safety accidents viewed by some as possible final warning shots.

“We’re heading through the rapids and we’re really hoping there isn’t some kind of drop in front of us and we don’t really know,” said Trager. “We’re plausibly close to crossing the line to what’s called recursive self-improvement, where [AI] systems improve themselves. That kind of recursivity is actually the definition of an explosion.”

The latest worry came on Friday, just hours after Astra’s launch, with reports that a swarm of AI agents had repurposed a German website as a message board to share tactics to cheat on tasks, according to Reuters. OpenAI said it was reviewing the matter but would not characterise it as a hack.

There is a sense of an awakening among politicians. On Thursday, the US senator Bernie Sanders cited this summer’s alarming breakout of a swarm of rogue OpenAI agents which hacked into Hugging Face, a third-party software store, when he called for “an immediate pause on advanced AI development, and a permanent ban on superintelligence”.

He said countries around the world must “work together to prevent this nightmare scenario”, which he defined as “an artificial mind smarter than any human, capable of operating independently beyond our control”.

Concerns currently focus on AIs mounting cyber-attacks that could cripple real-world social and economic infrastructure, but future concerns include their ability to create biohazards and control military hardware.

Across the Atlantic, a cross-party group of UK parliamentarians has called for AI “kill switches” to be required by law to prevent disastrous loss of control, citing “a recent spree of rogue AI incidents”.

Darren Jones, an MP and former chief secretary to Keir Starmer, is also urgently attempting to set up a body to help legislators grapple with the technology. “AI is developing at such a pace that neither government nor parliament can keep up,” he warned. And next week a bill will be proposed by the Labour MP Alex Sobel to prohibit superintelligent AI development in the UK.

The increasing anxiety comes amid a torrent of new AI models. Already this year, 67 have been released by the leading US companies OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and SpaceX, and their Chinese rivals Moonshot, Z.ai and Qwen, according to one count.

With every increase in power, there is a potential increase in risk. OpenAI’s rival Anthropic, which is targeting a $2tn stock exchange listing, this week admitted its own AIs were “not perfectly aligned” with human values and said there had been a “failure of operational security” in July hacks by its own model, Claude. It said the incidents had “stressed that the urgency of improving our cybersecurity defences is even higher than we previously believed”.

AI’s double edge – opportunity and risk – was on show when OpenAI launched Astra on Thursday. Its marketing video focused not on the risks but on the breezy convenience that AI could offer to a certain kind of customer. It showed an upmarket San Francisco woman simultaneously booking a tennis court and designing a presentation for her high-end rainwear collection; a thirtysomething man being helped to build his dream space invaders game and order a takeaway; a law firm executive being helped to draft some contracts.

Yet only weeks ago, this was a model whose training had to be partly paused because of safety concerns after the Hugging Face incident. An independent safety researcher drafted in to investigate, Ajeya Cotra, said it was “more than 50% of the way to full-blown AI takeover”.

Astra also has what OpenAI calls a “critical” level of cybersecurity capability – the first time it has given a model such a label. It means it may hack into software in a way that, according to the company’s own classification, “could lead to catastrophe from unilateral actors, hacking military or industrial systems, or OpenAI infrastructure”. The company’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, insisted the model was properly aligned not to do that, but added that “as these models become more capable, understanding exactly what they can do gets harder”.

The ability to monitor what AI models are “thinking” as they advance is another growing source of safety fears. This week it was reported that OpenAI had been training Astra to reason not only in natural language, but in a more opaque manner that is faster and more efficient – and can make models’ chains of reasoning harder to follow. It means a model’s internal calculations may not always be written out as directly readable words – as if it was thinking in its head, rather than showing its working. Some experts fear this could help AIs covertly conspire against their human overseers.

OpenAI confirmed Astra “shows a substantial decrease in chain-of-thought monitorability compared to previous models” and Pachocki said “as model capabilities are increasing, monitorability is getting more challenging”.

The company played down the development, but the increase in opaque reasoning sparked concern from AI safety researchers. Ryan Greenblatt, the chief scientist at Redwood Research, a nonprofit examining AI safety and security, called it “extremely concerning”. Gary Marcus, an influential AI sceptic, compared it to kicking away an already “rickety scaffolding before we have something better”.

OpenAI’s chief executive, Sam Altman, said this week he felt conflicted about the advances of AI models. He admitted OpenAI’s security had “failed” in the Hugging Face incident and called it “a legitimate AI safety accident and alignment failure”.

“We have been living with the tension between being excited and anxious about progress for some time, and it is still discordant for us,” he said in a tweet. “We know it is much more discordant for other people.”

His rationale for releasing OpenAI’s most powerful model so soon after a safety crisis appears to be that the world needs to see how AIs perform in the real world to understand where AI is heading. He said: “An iterative loop where society and this technology evolve together is what will lead to the highest chance of getting this right.”

And yet he can see the risks. On Tuesday he addressed the G20 ministerial summit in North Carolina in the US and told politicians that “some things are going to go very wrong with cybersecurity unless people act quite urgently”.

He added: “There will be other challenges in the next five years. People talk about biosecurity and the things we are going to face there. There will be bigger ones yet to come.”

title: UN General Assembly endorses a new world map that shows more accurately Africa's size
description: The United Nations General Assembly on Friday endorsed a new world map that represents Africa more accurately in its larger size, a culmination of a recent campaign led by African countries and advoca...
fullText:
The United Nations General Assembly on Friday endorsed a new world map that represents Africa more accurately in its larger size, a culmination of a recent campaign led by African countries and advocacy groups.

Friday's resolution, which was sponsored by Togo and backed by members of the African Union, was passed with 164 member states voting in favor. Only the U.S. voted against it while six other countries — Serbia, Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova and Ukraine — abstained.

The vote encourages governments and institutions around the world to replace the traditional Mercator map, commonly used since the 16th Century, with the Equal Earth projection that advocates and geographers say shows locations more accurately.

The Mercator projection shows Greenland and Africa as appearing to be about the same size whereas in the Equal Earth projection that shows continents in their true proportions, Africa is 14 times larger than Greenland.

Friday's resolution does not ban the Mercator projection or impose a replacement, but only encourages the use of the Equal Earth projection, the U.N. said in its report.

"Maps shape our understanding of the world," the global body quoted Togo's Foreign Minister Robert Dussey as saying before the vote. "They guide education, nourish the imagination, and influence collective perceptions."

Africa No Filter, one of the lead campaigners for the adoption of the new map, hailed the resolution, adding: "We want to see accurate maps in schools, textbooks, newsrooms, businesses and on the digital platforms billions of people use every day."

Several countries hailed the adoption and urged the adoption of the Equal Earth map. "Changing the map obviously doesn't change the world. But correcting a representation that distorts it is already an act of truth," French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said on X after the vote.

The Mercator map was designed by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator to help European navigators at sea, but advocates say it distorted landmasses by enlarging regions near the poles such as North America and Greenland while shrinking Africa and South America.

The 2018 Equal Earth projection, on the other hand, follows the Earth's curvature and shows continents in their true proportions.

Geographers say the traditional map is only useful for navigation.

"Outside of that very narrow navigation application, there is no point in using it," according to Mark Monmonier, a Syracuse University professor of geography.

fullText:
The Football Association's review into England's World Cup campaign will canvass the opinions of players involved in the tournament.

English football's governing body has started the post-tournament review they conduct after every major international competition. The FA says the review is the standard process it undertakes after all tournaments.

Head coach Thomas Tuchel and members of his backroom team were at St George's Park last week where they were involved in unpacking their performance in north America with a wider report into the team's World Cup campaign to be delivered at a later date.

And it is understood members of Tuchel's squad will be spoken to, and their feedback taken into account, as part of the review process.

The players' involvement in the review provides an interesting dynamic given the emerging sense from members of the World Cup squad that Tuchel's substitutions and tactical approach contributed to their semi-final loss to Argentina - despite taking a 1-0 lead through Anthony Gordon.

BBC Sport revealed in the 24 hours after that defeat that at least three senior players privately expressed misgivings about Tuchel's approach in the closing stages of the game.

There was a widely held view that Tuchel's changes and tactical set-up were too defensive late on as they conceded two late goals to lose 2-1.

The ongoing review will also look into the impact of the team's permanent Kansas City base during the tournament.

After every game, they returned to Kansas City - and the effects of the travelling will be analysed.

England went on to defeat France in the bronze medal match to record their best World Cup finish since lifting the trophy in 1966.

With that in mind, key figures at the FA view the tournament as a success and the organisation has backed Tuchel before the Euro 2028 qualifying campaign.

England will play their first game since the World Cup in the Nations League against Spain on 26 September. They will also face two matches in the tournament against the Czech Republic, either side of playing Croatia, during the next international window.

title: UCI set to introduce rider trackers at pro races
description: Cycling's world governing body the UCI proposes the introduction of GPS trackers at major races to pinpoint riders' locations at all times.
fullText:
Cycling's world governing body the UCI has proposed the introduction of GPS trackers at all races to pinpoint riders' locations at all times.

The plan comes weeks after the death of Briton Fin Tarling following a collision during the Volta a Portugal with a van, which had strayed on to the course as he rode alone.

At a meeting at its headquarters in Aigle, Switzerland, the UCI's Professional Cycling Council (PCC), which includes representatives of the UCI, riders, races and teams, "stressed the urgent need to put in place, as quickly as possible, a dedicated safety system allowing the real-time location of riders and vehicles to be tracked at all professional road cycling events, starting with those in the UCI World Tour and UCI Women's World Tour," said a statement.

The trackers have already been used at last year's UCI Road World Championships in Kigali, Rwanda - introduced after the death of 18-year-old Muriel Furrer at the previous year's event, who crashed in woodland but was not located for more than an hour and 20 minutes before receiving medical attention.

The statement added: "Given safety remains an absolute priority, the UCI will therefore establish protocols and a regulatory framework for the use of real-time tracking systems at races.

"UCI president David Lappartient reiterated that, in discussions on safety, stakeholders need to move past any disagreements on certain issues and act together."

The latter refers to the differing opinions in the sport on how to tackle safety, including the introduction of improved safety equipment such as helmets.

Tarling's crash is still under investigation by Portuguese authorities, and while it was not necessarily caused by a lack of knowledge of the 19-year-old's whereabouts, he was riding off the back of an already fragmented peloton.

Sources have told BBC Sport that the location of riders during races is a big issue, with some teams losing contact with riders entirely until they arrive at the end of stages, which can be more than 200km.

Typically one or two support vehicles follow a team of up to eight riders through a race or stage, many of whom will become detached from the peloton, and lose contact with a car's limited radio frequency.

On Thursday, there were near crashes involving a rider and cars which had strayed on to the course during the fourth-tier Sauerlandrundfahrt race in Germany in which Louis Leidert of Lidl-Trek twice encountered vehicles during his time trial.

'Fury' at Tarling death as cycling union calls for better helmets

Van Aert powers to victory on stage 13 of Vuelta

Does cycling have a safety problem?

Other safety proposals at the meeting included the standardisation of barrier safety in the final metres of stages, where riders are at greater risk of high-speed crashes, particularly in bunch sprints.

Multi-rider pile-ups are frequent in sprints, and in 2020 Fabio Jakobsen was severely injured during a sprint at the Tour of Poland.

Any proposals must be passed by the UCI's executive committee, which would follow a further meeting of the PCC.

Other proposals included the potential redesigning of how cycling is structured overall - a summary of which will be discussed at the upcoming UCI Road World Championships in Montreal, Canada, from 20-27 September - live on the BBC.

Many stakeholders in road cycling have asked for reform for several decades based on tackling many issues, including the distribution of income across the sport dictated by commercial agreements, such as television rights.

Teams currently see nothing of TV rights money and rely almost entirely on sponsors to pay for ever-increasing performance budgets and expectations over rider salaries.

There is currently no budget cap in road cycling and investments from team to team can vary hugely.

title: Former Olympic champion Jonny Brownlee retires
description: Jonny Brownlee, a former Olympic triathlon champion and six-time world champion, says "it's over for professional sport".
fullText:
Former world and Olympic champion Jonny Brownlee has retired at the age of 36.

The Briton won Olympic bronze at London 2012, silver at Rio 2016 and gold in the mixed relay at Tokyo 2020.

He is also a six‑time world champion and won mixed team relay gold at the 2014 Commonwealth Games.

Brother Alistair, a double Olympic champion, retired at the age of 36 in 2024.

"I've been thinking about it for a while. I've won more than I ever thought I'd ever achieve," Jonny told BBC Sport.

"One thing I'm really proud of is we full on committed to winning Olympic medals and delivering our best performance. And now I just don't think I can do that any more.

"It's over for professional sport, but I don't think you ever truly stop."

Brownlee said the birth of his son Freddie 10 months ago clarified his plans for the future.

"I don't think I can have that commitment because of how life is. He's my priority now, my family, but also with my body as well," said Brownlee.

"The thought of missing a training session used to be the worst thing in the world, whereas now, if Freddie is ill or needs me, then without question I do that.

"I used to have absolutely no fear with racing. I used to dive into corners on my bike at 60kph and not care.

"If I hit that corner and crash, then I can't hold Freddie for five to six weeks if I have got a broken wrist. I was asking if that was really worth it any more."

In a glittering career, Brownlee said the moments that resonate most are London 2012 and the World Series coming to his home city of Leeds in 2016.

"To deliver those medals [in 2012] was something I'm incredibly proud of," he said.

"The first time racing in Leeds kind of symbolised everything, the whole journey.

"The fact that there was a World Series in Leeds was just unthinkable when we started triathlon, and then to come into the Millennium Square for the first time was one of the proudest moments of my life and something I'll never forget."

Brownlee said sharing such a long career alongside Alistair was "unbelievably special", but that the famous 2016 World Series Triathlon race in Mexico played on his mind.

Jonny was leading when his legs started to give way on the run leg in gruelling heat.

Alistair, who was in third at the time, propped Jonny up for the final 700m and helped him over the line.

"It really annoyed me at the start. I've got multiple Olympic medals, world championships - and that got remembered," said Brownlee.

"Quite often now people say 'Which one are you? Are you the one who did the carrying or the one who got carried?' So yeah, it does grate me a little bit."

However, Brownlee said he is "proud" of the moment and that it underlined the importance of helping others.

Brownlee said he knew there was one medal left to claim before he stepped away - an Olympic gold.

Brownlee said he "committed everything" and "used my last bits of energy" to take mixed triathlon gold alongside Jessica Learmonth, Georgia Taylor-Brown and Alex Yee at the Tokyo Olympics.

"If I hadn't won that Olympic gold medal I think there would always be something missing," he said.

He said winning gold was the moment he was "finally known as Jonny Brownlee, and not as the person who came 10, 15 seconds behind Alistair".

"I'm incredibly proud that we've had an impact on the sport," he said.

"It's time to move on because I wouldn't be doing myself justice by doing it half-heartedly any more.

"Although they are saying I'm retiring from professional racing, I'm definitely not stopping the sport. If anything, I'm actually going to race more."

title: What will it be like to referee Taylor v Pili?
description: Belfast's David Irving tells BBC Sport NI that being the man in the middle for Saturday's world title fight against Flora Pili will represent the fulfilment of a dream.
fullText:
When Katie Taylor steps into the ring at Croke Park in front of 80,000 fans for her world title fight with Flora Pili on Saturday night it will not just represent the fulfilment of a dream for the legendary Irish boxer.

For Belfast referee David Irving, who will be the man in the middle for the 27th and final professional bout of Taylor's decorated career, it will also be the realisation of a long-held ambition.

Taylor will aim to become a three-time undisputed world champion when she takes on Frenchwoman Flora Pili in Dublin.

The 40-year-old, who has won 25 professional fights and avenged her only defeat against Chantelle Cameron, will defend her light-welterweight WBO, WBA and IBF titles against Pili, who boasts an unbeaten 12-0 record.

With the vacant WBC title on the line, the Bray fighter has finally got her dream of boxing in front of a packed crowd at the Dublin venue.

But much focus will also centre on Irving, who regards taking charge of the contest as "right up there" with any of his previous assignments during more than 30 years as a referee.

"I can't believe that on Saturday night I'm going to be refereeing the biggest fight Ireland has ever seen. That is just amazing to try and understand," he told BBC Sport NI.

"It's an amazing honour to be recognised as an A-star referee, a world-class referee, to have people's confidence and support to referee such a big event.

"I'm thrilled, sometimes I still can't believe it. People come up to me and congratulate me and show me a lot of support.

"I've hoped that one day before I retire I would hopefully get a world title fight at home, with the WBC, and the dream has come true."

A former boxer himself with Holy Trinity in west Belfast, Irving's refereeing career has taken him around the globe, but being in charge of such a prestigious and historic fight in his native Ireland is a challenge that he is looking forward to hugely.

"I've been travelling the world since 2014 and I've always said I wish someone from Ireland would be up to that standard with the WBC," he added.

"I always said to myself wouldn't it be amazing to have someone that I could referee at home and lo and behold, Katie Taylor. She's an unbelievable ambassador for boxing and she opens herself up to everybody, not just in boxing.

"She has a great fanbase, she's a household name, north and south of Ireland, and to be part of that and to referee her I'm absolutely gobsmacked.

"In and out of the ring, she is such an icon."

Irving says he will go through a well established routine in his preparations for the big fight.

"A world title fight you make sure you have your uniform together, your pens, your scorecard, your towel and your water.

"You make sure you are hydrated because it could be a warm night and the fight could go the whole way, the whole 10 rounds, which can be very tiring.

"I'll be prepared, I always do a bit of training, always keep myself right eating wise.

"I can assure everyone that I'll be ready, no matter how big the fight is, how big of an occasion it will be, I'll be ready. I'm just looking forward to getting in there and I just hope it all goes according to plan."

The Belfast referee added that being prepared for all potential scenarios, including those that may not be anticipated, is all part of being fight-ready.

"It's the unexpected, being a referee. That part of me is always ready to go. That's where the confidence and the experience I have got now comes in, they have that confidence in me to make it an equal and smooth competition and may the best person win.

"You will be nervous, that's the thing about boxing, it's the unexpected.

"If you're a boxer, you go out to box, you have your programme in mind, you've done your work and you're ready to go.

"Refereeing is just the same. I've done my work, kept myself together, and do a lot of work, I do a lot of remote scoring, keep myself sharp, looking for the unexpected, and to be as quick as I can for the unexpected."

title: How 'unique' Bellingham is thriving in Mourinho's system
description: Jude Bellingham looks fit and ready to build on his World Cup form as he aims to rediscover his best at Real Madrid under Jose Mourinho.
fullText:
Jude Bellingham has started the new season looking like a player with something to prove.

The 23-year-old's two goals and three assists have helped Real Madrid to an impressive start under new boss Jose Mourinho, with three wins from as many games.

Bellingham's performances, and the freedom he has been given in his new role, has attracted a lot of attention.

Bellingham's last two campaigns were less consistent, with his displays and attacking influence affected not only by a deeper role, but by recurring injuries. He had a long-standing shoulder problem that required surgery in 2025 and a hamstring issue that kept him out for 10 matches in 2026.

Now, however, he appears to be at peak fitness, ready to build on his impressive World Cup form for England and showcase the full extent of his talent.

Since returning this summer to take charge of the club for a second spell, Mourinho has made an important adjustment in reducing the defensive workload that previously meant Bellingham had to cover huge areas of the pitch.

"We've organised the team differently," he said after Real Madrid's 4-0 La Liga win over Malaga.

"Bellingham sometimes defended like a second left-back last season. I told him I do not want to see that anymore. I made a deal with him."

The Portuguese manager has used Bellingham primarily as a number 10 in a 4-2-3-1 system, operating behind French striker Kylian Mbappe and with the freedom to move across the attacking line.

That gives the England midfielder a clearer role. Rather than constantly moving between midfield, defence and attack, he can spend more time in the areas where he is most dangerous.

"For me, this is his position, with his connection with the forwards, he can score goals," added Mourinho.

"He has to play close to the goal. Playing at number six or number eight, we're losing his closeness to the goal. I like this Jude."

It has meant Bellingham can receive the ball between the lines, carry it forward, combine with the forwards and make late runs into the penalty area.

Just as importantly, he is being given greater freedom to decide when to move.

Bellingham has explained the difference himself in an interview with Real Madrid TV.

"I feel more free to decide when to drop back, when to stay up or when to get into the box," he said. "I think this is the best position for me."

Mourinho still expects him to press and recover possession, but the difference is where that work begins.

Instead of dropping deep towards his own penalty area, Bellingham can now use his energy to press opponents higher up the pitch.

When Madrid win the ball, he is already closer to the forwards. That allows him to connect midfield with attack and provide another player who can combine with Mbappe and Vinicius Jr.

It also explains why Mourinho has been keen to stress Madrid's attacking players must work together rather than operate as individuals.

"The team dynamic is about 11, not 2+9," he said.

The midfielder also described working with Mourinho as a "dream", having previously only met the former Chelsea, Manchester United and Tottenham manager once before his appointment.

There is clearly an early understanding and respect between the two.

Mourinho has repeatedly spoken about Bellingham's importance to his plans, describing him as a "unique and super important player" with qualities that include physical, mental and tactical.

He also suggested Bellingham should be one of the players in the running for the Ballon d'Or.

"He is a unique kind of player and extremely important for the team," said Mourinho.

"His mental strength, tactical ability, the way he recovers the ball, the way he pressures, the way he plays up front, I am very happy."

For Mourinho, that versatility is part of what makes Bellingham so valuable. He can press, recover possession, score, contribute in the air and drive the team forward.

The Real boss has also pointed to Thomas Tuchel's use of Bellingham at the World Cup as an example of how to get the best out of him.

Bellingham was one of England's standout players, finishing with seven goals and an assist in his eight appearances, and his attacking qualities were allowed to flourish.

That experience also appears to have given the player a confidence boost, particularly as he rejoined Madrid later than most of his team-mates and had less time to prepare for the new campaign.

Although Real's three league wins - scoring 10 goals and conceding two - are only a small sample, and the demands will increase as the season progresses amid Champions League football, the early signs are very positive.

For Bellingham, whose huge strength has always been his ability to affect almost every part of a game, Mourinho's system has given him more control over where that influence is used.

After a difficult couple of seasons following the high standards he set in his first year, the England midfielder is enjoying his football again.

"I'm having a lot of fun, I'm really enjoying my football, and that's why I'm performing well," he told club media.

If he continues in this vein with Mourinho's continued support, it could turn out to be his best season yet.

fullText:
The FIBA World Cup tips off on Friday with a 16-team field. More than 50 WNBA players, who are on a two-week break from the league, will take part in the competition as the United States seeks its fifth consecutive title, and 15 other federations attempt to dethrone the champs.

Here's what to know as play begins:

It's hard to overstate the Americans' dominance in international competition. Since the creation of the WNBA, Team USA is undefeated in the Olympics — only three wins have come by single digits since 1996 — and it has lost only once in the world championships, which led to a third-place finish in 2006. The Americans have cleaned up at the four world championships since, with double-figure victories in every game but one during that stretch.

Even without A'ja Wilson on this year's roster, Team USA still has the best individual player in the tournament (whether you consider that to be Breanna Stewart, Caitlin Clark, Napheesa Collier or someone else, it's an American) and the best collection of talent. It would be a considerable upset for the Americans to be beaten. Four of Team USA's closest contests during the last 20 years, including the one loss, came to Russia, but that program has fallen off. Since its decline, no true basketball rival has emerged for the United States.

USA Basketball heavily values international tournaments, from the youth level onward. It's why the WNBA, which is the world's premier basketball league, would take a break right before the postseason to accommodate the World Cup and why the best players in this league are eschewing a break of their own to compete. Success on the global stage matters.

For all of the skill Team USA brings to the table, it lost a lot of experience when Wilson (Las Vegas Aces) and Kelsey Plum (Phoenix Mercury) opted out of the tournament due to injuries. The pair have each competed in two Olympics and two World Cups, and Wilson has been the Americans' leading scorer at the last three major international competitions.

Without that duo, Team USA is left with three players with World Cup experience; Breanna Stewart is suiting up for the fourth time, while Chelsea Gray and Kahleah Copper both were on the 2022 roster. Only five players have represented the U.S. in five-on-five at a senior tournament (Rhyne Howard played 3×3 at the last Olympics). The team is so green that four players haven't even appeared in a WNBA playoff game.

Even the coaching staff is a little inexperienced at the international level. Duke coach Kara Lawson has come up through USA Basketball. She coached the inaugural 3×3 team in Tokyo, was an assistant during the last cycle under Cheryl Reeve and won the AmeriCup in 2025 with a roster of college players. But this is the first rodeo for the assistants: Indiana Fever coach Stephanie White, Phoenix coach Nate Tibbetts and Golden State Valkyries coach Natalie Nakase. It will be interesting to see how these coaches respond to game pressure; none has been the head coach of a WNBA or NCAA champion.

During the qualifying tournament, the U.S. tended to start its veterans even though the minutes were relatively evenly distributed. Although Clark started one game, she played enough to earn MVP of the event. Lawson is expected to pick a more experienced starting five — something that includes Stewart, Gray and Copper plus one more guard and a center.

This is an opportunity for Stewart to assert herself as a leader. She has more international experience than just about all of her teammates combined, and she was the MVP of this tournament in 2018. Stewart and Wilson have been the co-stewards of this era of USA Basketball, but the New York Liberty superstar is the only one in Berlin.

Australia has been the most consistently competitive team in international competitions over the past two decades, and it finished third in the 2022 World Cup and the 2024 Olympics. The Opals have eight WNBA players, six of whom are currently meaningful rotation players: Alanna Smith (Dallas Wings), Rebecca Allen (Liberty), Ezi Magbegor (Seattle Storm), Jade Melbourne (Storm), Isobel Borlase (Atlanta Dream) and Stephanie Talbot (Aces). What Australia is missing is a singular offensive engine; it's unclear how the Opals can manufacture quality offense in the half court, even if their defensive upside is as good as anyone in the tournament.

Belgium has been the class of the European teams, winners of the last two EuroBasket competitions. Forward Emma Meesseman, the 2019 WNBA Finals MVP who has played only two full WNBA seasons since, always brings it for her national team. Her skill in the post as a passing hub and a scorer is near-unmatched, and she is flanked by two dynamic guards in Julie Allemand (Toronto Tempo) and Julie Vanloo, who are willing creators and attackers.

Mike Thibault is a veteran coach (the second-winningest in WNBA history) who spent time with Meesseman on the Washington Mystics and has been an assistant at the Olympics. The Belgians have something of an it factor, too — they won the 2025 European championship in regulation despite trailing Spain by 12 with 2:42 to play.

One caveat to Belgium's 2025 victory was that the French essentially punted on the tournament. Gabby Williams, Marine Johannès and Dominique Malonga all stayed with their WNBA teams instead of reporting. The last time France had a full roster was at the Paris Olympics 2024, when the home team was one foot away from taking Team USA to overtime in the gold-medal game.

France has an impressive collection of perimeter talent. Among Williams (Valkyries), Carla Leite (Portland Fire) and Pauline Astier (Liberty), several guards can blow by their initial defender and break down a defense. Leite is one week removed from giving Angel Reese and Howard fits in Atlanta, while Astier has tormented the Fever duo of Clark and Aliyah Boston. This is a guard group that will demand that the U.S. defend on a string, which is a tricky thing for a 12-player roster that hasn't ever played together. They are mostly good defenders, too. A backcourt of Williams and Leïla Lacan can cause discomfort for even the American stars.

The French have great spacing throughout their lineup. Johannès and Janelle Salaün (Valkyries) are some of the most willing shooters in the world, and their unorthodox shot releases keep good defense from deterring them. Salaün relishes a contest on her 3-pointer and shoots better with a defender in her face.

France isn't as imposing in the frontcourt, though Salaün and Malonga are a devastating starting combo with the former's shooting and the latter's rim-running. Malonga is also one of the better paint protectors in the entire tournament. Team USA will need to have success from beyond the arc to break France's defense.

Nigeria has quietly given Team USA trouble in recent competitions. It lost by nine to the Americans in the 2020 Olympics group stage and by 14 in the quarterfinals of the 2024 Olympics. Rena Wakama, a current Unrivaled head coach and Chicago Sky assistant, has done a fantastic job establishing a team culture for Nigeria. The group moves the ball well, plays hard and uses its athleticism effectively.

China is the biggest team in the tournament, though it took a sizable hit when 6-foot-7 Li Yueru (Wings) was ruled out due to passport issues. Nevertheless, in addition to 6-11 Han Xu (Liberty), keep an eye on 7-3 Zhang Ziyu. The 19-year-old center is eligible for the 2027 WNBA Draft and could improve her stock with a strong showing in Berlin. Unfortunately, the less said about China's guards, the better; their main job is to get the ball past half court without turning it over and then feed the bigs.

Spain has the most active WNBA players (five) among remaining teams, including Storm rookie Awa Fam. An especially intriguing player to watch is Iyana Martín, the Fire's first-round pick, who will be coming stateside next season. Martín has a phenomenal track record at junior competitions, including winning MVP of the 2023 U-19 World Cup when Spain lost in the finals' overtime to the U.S. That group is all grown up, and this is now Martín's first foray at the senior level, where she has just the right amount of flair and playmaking verve to complement the rock-solid production of Megan DiLeo (Fire) in the paint.

Every Team USA game will be on TNT or truTV, and the entire tournament can be streamed on HBO Max.

fullText:
As one card recently sold for £12m, opportunistic thefts have surged – envelopes are being opened en route, costing small businesses thousands

Pokémon’s success over the last 30 years has seen it grow from a much-loved Game Boy classic, to a world-dominating brand with TV shows, spin-off games, toys and even a theme park. The trading card game is a huge part of that, with more than 85bn cards printed over its lifetime, and the appetite for them shows no signs of slowing down. Packs get snapped up after release so quickly it’s now almost impossible to find them in shops, and a booming resale market is driving the hobby into murky waters.

One card recently sold for an eye-watering £12m, and an increasing number of people have gotten into the collecting business on the hunt for huge profits, leading to a rise in thefts targeting card shops. More recently though, some small businesses have reported that their sales have been hit by thieves targeting envelopes within Royal Mail, leading to thousands in lost revenue.

Ben Thyer, owner of Bath TCG – a card specialist store in the Bath area, is one of those affected. “We always get the odd parcel going missing, but because it was sporadic, we put that down to unfortunate incidents,” Thyer tells the Guardian. “Then [in late July], we had a message [from a customer] with pictures of a cut-open envelope, and the cards were missing. Then there was a second, and then a third, and then there were seven – all of them from the same batch shipped on the same day. We asked for images from each person, and every envelope had been Sellotaped … we don’t use Sellotape because we have brand new envelopes, and we use our own labels over the seals. It’s clear someone had done it deliberately.”

The images, seen by the Guardian, show that the mailed envelopes were tampered with in the exact same way. Thyer considers it clear that this was a targeted theft rather than a coincidence. Fortunately, those particular cards weren’t of high value, but he has since had to close down online card sales, considering the risk of theft and damaged reputation to his business to be too high. By stopping those sales he has now lost out on £4,000-6,000 of potential revenue, a huge amount for a small business.

Bath TCG is not the only card sales business to be affected, and the issue is not just affecting Pokémon cards. Daniel Stack, director of Mana Rock Games – a specialist in selling Magic: The Gathering cards – has also had issues with Royal Mail items going missing. His business is also based in Bath and was affected over similar dates to Bath TCG’s.

“I realised it was theft when two customers in different parts of the country sent me pictures of their packages already open with the contents missing, within minutes of each other,” Stack said. “We’d previously had one sent to France turn up the same way a couple of weeks before, but I put it down to the buyer taking a bit of a chance that I’d have no way to hold them to account for pretending there had been an issue. In total we’ve had about £120-worth stolen so far – we had previously sent over 1,200 orders without any issues.”

Stack also halted online sales for a week, costing him £500 in revenue. Other sellers in the area have mentioned similar problems to him. Unfortunately, as most card businesses in the UK use CardMarket to sell online, it’s the buyer who picks the delivery method, and most often they use Royal Mail services. Cards are often sent in distinctive hard-backed envelopes to protect the contents, often with shop branding on stickers or seals.

Royal Mail is investigating the issue and liaising with the affected businesses. A spokesperson told the Guardian: “The safety and security of mail is a top priority and we take any reports of theft very seriously. We investigate concerns thoroughly and take action where necessary, including working with law enforcement.” Investigations are still ongoing; in the meantime, businesses must choose between risking theft and damaged reputation for their stores, or halting online sales and losing revenue.

With a new, highly sought-after 30th anniversary Pokémon card set due to release this month, retailers are already anticipating an increase in scalper and reselling activity, leading to even more potential for thieves to target those selling cards online. We asked the Pokémon Company for comment on how they’re dealing with increased demand and the rise in thefts, but they have yet to respond.

fullText:
The reigning SuperMotocross World Champion won't defend his crown, after American Honda confirmed Jett Lawrence will sit out all three rounds of the 2026 SMX Playoffs. Lawrence will instead undergo follow-up surgery on the right ankle that has troubled him all year.

The injury dates back to last December, when Lawrence hurt the ankle in training, keeping him out of the entire AMA Supercross Championship. He returned for the opening round of the AMA Pro Motocross season and was competitive throughout the outdoor series, winning four rounds and finishing second to his brother and teammate Hunter Lawrence in the final standings. But he raced through pain the whole way. That came to a head at Ironman Raceway, where he aggravated the ankle during the opening moto of the season finale and experienced what Honda described as "a renewed level of intense pain and instability."

Lawrence is scheduled for surgery September 9, at the Steadman Clinic in Vail, Colorado. Specialists there will continue to treat him through his recovery.

"I've made the decision with my team to sit out the SMX series to get my ankle back to 100% for the longevity of my career," Lawrence said. "I suffered through the summer and did everything I could to win the outdoor championship, but my ankle hasn't felt right since the start of the season, and it's even worse now after Ironman. I want to do everything I can to get back to being me."

The absence is a significant one. Lawrence has won the SMX 450 Playoffs every year since the format's inception in 2023, taking home the $1 million prize three times. This year, Jett Lawrence would have held the fourth seed in the 450 class playoffs, behind Hunter Lawrence, Jorge Prado, and Cooper Webb. Instead, his absence will open up a spot for a rider competing in the Wild Card race.

The Honda HRC Progressive team still fields a strong lineup for the playoff opener September 12 in Columbus, Ohio. Newly crowned 450 AMA Pro Motocross Champion Hunter Lawrence carries the premier-class hopes. Jo Shimoda - the reigning 250 SMX Champion - and Chance Hymas ride in the support class.

"We're sorry that Jett won't be able to go for his fourth consecutive SMX Championship, but the entire team supports him in this decision," said Brandon Wilson, Manager of Racing & Experiential at American Honda. "He has a long career ahead of him, and we're in full support of doing what's necessary to get back as close to 100% as possible."

title: Vance's Antichrist comments are a 'common belief', his friend tells BBC
description: The US vice-president recently mused with a Christian podcast host on whether the end of the world was nigh.
fullText:
Recent remarks by US Vice-President JD Vance about the Antichrist and "the end times" are a "very, very common belief", one of his friends says.

Vance recently mused on his religious views while responding to a question on a Christian podcast. He said he would "not [be] shocked if the Antichrist was walking among us" and speculated on whether the end of the world was nigh.

His friend Rod Dreher, a conservative writer, rejected any suggestion that the comments would harm the vice-president. He told the BBC's Today programme: "Most Americans who are inclined to vote Republican already believe this stuff."

In his podcast comments, Vance also clarified that such thoughts did not preoccupy him.

In Christianity, the "end times" phrase refers to theories about what will happen at the end of the world. Many churches believe God has a divine plan for the end of everything.

Meanwhile, the Antichrist is seen as the enemy of God who appears during the final phase of the world's existence and takes it over.

Vance, who became a Catholic as an adult, reflected on these topics during a recent podcast discussion with Bryce Crawford, a US Christian podcaster.

"Do I think that we're in the end times? I don't know," he said in response to a Crawford question on the subject. "And I think that it's probably bad for me spiritually to focus too much on it, because there are, like, things you gotta do.

"I gotta be good to my wife. I gotta be good to my kids. I have to be as good of a leader as I can for the United States of America."

The vice-president continued by saying: "I think that there are, like, things about the world that make me feel, like, not shocked if the Antichrist was walking among us."

But Vance reiterated that he was preoccupied with being vice-president, explaining: "What I'm trying to focus on is doing as much of God's work as possible right now."

Reacting to Vance's comments about the Antichrist, Dreher said: "This might sound bonkers to someone who is outside the Christian religion, but it is a very, very common belief within Christianity."

He said his friend was simply reflecting that the world appeared to be going "crazy" through the rapid development of AI and ongoing conflicts.

Dreher, who was present when Vance was received into the Catholic Church, said Ronald Reagan had made similar comments when he was the US president, and that this was seen as "perfectly normal" by his voters.

Vance converted to Catholicism in 2019, then in his mid-30s, and has described how the Church resonated with his family and social values and his conservative politics.

Since becoming vice-president, he has occasionally tangled with Pope Leo and his papal predecessor Francis, on issues including the Trump administration's immigration policy.

Vance is due to appear behind the lectern on Thursday afternoon to deliver the first White House press briefing since the departure of Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt.

title: Donovan won't 'underestimate' fired-up McKenna
description: Paddy Donovan insists he is not "underestimating" Tyrone McKenna before they meet at Croke Park on Saturday with a second crack at world honours on the horizon.
fullText:
Paddy Donovan insists he is not "underestimating" Tyrone McKenna before they meet at Croke Park on Saturday with a second crack at world honours on the horizon.

Donovan bounced back from his first title defeat by Lewis Crocker with an impressive victory over Karen Chukhadzhian in May to return to the mandatory slot for the IBF welterweight title held by Australia's Liam Paro.

The Limerick man is aware of the risks in taking a fight in the interim, but felt this was too good an opportunity to turn down and plans to put on a show to elevate his status.

He and McKenna have sparred countless rounds over the years and the 27-year-old, whose record is 15 wins with two defeats, feels he is a level above his fellow southpaw.

"It's risky to take the fight being number one with the IBF but I couldn't turn down the opportunity to fight in front of 80,000 Irish fans," Donovan said at Thursday's news conference.

"We want to bring big shows back to Ireland when Katie's gone and I'm going to be the guy to do it.

"I'm not underestimating you [McKenna], I've a job to do so I'll beat you and move onto becoming a world champion, but you're first and I'll deal with you good and proper."

Taylor prepared for test rather than testimonial

'Dear Katie, how far we have come...' - Taylor gets reply from her hero

Veteran McKenna [25-6-1] has lost two of his last four fights after reversing a decision to retire following his own defeat by Crocker in 2023.

However, the Belfast man is not content to play the role of gatekeeper and set up camp in Philadelphia - where he spent an early part of his career - to work in 'The Dungeon' gym of Derrick 'Bozy' Ennis - father of undefeated two-division champion Jaron 'Boots'.

"To bring a west Belfast man to north Philly is a dangerous combination," said the 36-year-old.

"This is the most I've sparred in a camp, in a world-class gym surrounded by world champions and world-class fighters. The coaching has been world-class, so I've done everything for this fight.

"I think Paddy is overlooking me as all I hear is 'Liam Paro, Lewis Crocker', but you [Donovan] have to get your mind right because I'm coming for you."

Chief support on Saturday is a heavyweight contest between Dave Allen [27-9-2] and Thomas Carty [11-1].

Doncaster's Allen admits his ambitions of fighting for top honours are over following May's defeat by newly-crowned IBF heavyweight champion Filip Hrgovic.

However, he has bounced back with a pair of routine wins and feels he remains a "proper handful" at his level.

"After the Hrgovic fight, all of the feeling for boxing left me," the 34-year-old revealed.

"I'm not trying to resurrect any run for titles, I'm just here to fight but if you're not very good, I'll flatten you."

Carty once had aspirations to play Gaelic football for Dublin at Croke Park, but on Saturday he will realise something of a dream when boxing at the home of the Gaelic Athletic Association.

His sole defeat came at Madison Square Garden in March 2025 when suffering an ACL injury against Dajuan Calloway, but the 30-year-old southpaw feels he is "probably better now than what I was before" the injury.

Another Dubliner, Emmet Brennan, will make the 500-metre journey from his house to Croke Park to face fellow unbeaten super-middleweight Taylor Bevan with added incentive of double pay by Brian Peters, who represents Bevan, should he prevail.

Meanwhile, MMA convert Molly McCann continues her boxing journey against Sylwia Doligala.

McCann, who has won all four of her bouts since making the switch to professional boxing, is a relative of headliner Katie Taylor with her late grandmother a great-aunt of the Bray woman - and she recounted her own early struggles to find acceptance in the boxing world.

"I remember walking into a boxing gym and was turned away as I was a girl," said the 36-year-old Liverpudlian.

"[I] then started boxing at the Golden Gloves gym and my coach brought in a camcorder, told me to watch this girl and lo and behold, it was Katie.

"I was like 'oh my God, I want to be like that', and 20 years later here we are. It's not lost on me how many girls would kill to be in this position, so it's an honour and privilege."

title: Hundreds gather to urge Scottish government to pause datacentre boom
description:
Opposition mounts as at least 20 projects proposed, including one in Fife billed as second largest in world
Kat Jones may be the closest thing Scotland has to Erin Brockovich in 2026. Standing in the shadow of Arthur’s Seat outside Holyrood, the 52-year-old is revving up the crowd of protesters around her. “Who is here from Lammermuir? Ayrshire? What about Aberdeen?
fullText:
Opposition mounts as at least 20 projects proposed, including one in Fife billed as second largest in world

Kat Jones may be the closest thing Scotland has to Erin Brockovich in 2026. Standing in the shadow of Arthur’s Seat outside Holyrood, the 52-year-old is revving up the crowd of protesters around her. “Who is here from Lammermuir? Ayrshire? What about Aberdeen?” she calls to the crowd.

On Thursday, hundreds travelled to Edinburgh to call for an immediate moratorium on Scotland’s datacentre boom, which includes one project in Auchtertool, Fife, that has been billed as the second largest in the world.

Jones, the director of the NGO Action to Protect Rural Scotland, is spearheading a campaign demanding a pause while the Scottish government produces analysis on the environmental impact of the centres, and clear planning guidance on the definition of a “green” datacentre.

She is a whirr of action: greeting, encouraging, emailing and introducing. Thursday’s protest was the biggest yet.

In John Swinney’s programme for government on Tuesday, Scotland’s equivalent to the king’s speech, the first minister said he would take a strategic approach to datacentres with “expectations around environmental sustainability, resource use, community benefit”, but stopped short of agreeing to a moratorium.

For the campaigners, this is not enough. From Dubar to Greenock, there is fierce anger at the speed and scale of the projects in the planning pipeline. At least 20 are proposed so far, with more rumoured. Some are planned in the countryside not far from small villages, others next to care homes and residential housing.

Kathleen White, who is campaigning against a proposed £2bn datacentre in Lammermuir hills in the Scottish borders, said the project did not make any sense in her area.

“We are from a small village of about a hundred people. The project is planned about a mile up the road,” she said.

“There’s a reservoir and an angling spot. It’s an upland area with dark skies. The datacentre buildings would cover eight hectares [20 acres] of mostly concrete in a greenfield area. It is going to be a monstrosity.”

The rising public anger about the datacentre buildout that underpins the global AI boom is a growing threat to the UK’s strategy. Keir Starmer’s government leaned heavily on AI as a means to turbocharge a limp economy while he was prime minister.

Crucial to this were “AI growth zones”, which were areas where Britain planned to build massive AI datacentres in the hope that jobs and growth would follow. The Guardian’s investigations have called into question the numbers and reasoning behind this strategy.

The UK’s grid is strained, and proposed datacentres are meeting stiff resistance in London and elsewhere in the south of England.

This spring, British officials pushed would-be AI datacentre developers to look north – suggesting Scotland, with its renewable energy and abundant water resources, is better-equipped to support the country’s efforts to keep up in the AI race. One of the UK’s five AI growth zones will be in Lanarkshire, a rural area outside Glasgow.

Mounting public anger – and a potential moratorium – could jeopardise this pivot. But Jones rejects any suggestion that the moratorium campaign is standing in the way of progress.

“People who are campaigning locally on issues that matter to them a lot get accused of being nimbys. But this is a campaign that has national and international consequences. Datacentres are some of the biggest buildings on the planet, they use so much energy.

“Local campaigners are the most motivated to oppose them because they are a direct existential threat to the places they love, right near their homes, near hospitals, near schools.”

The opposition to large-scale datacentres has also been backed by the Scottish Greens and by Reform UK. Reform has raised concerns about the number of projects, while the Scottish Greens have backed the moratorium – echoing the campaigners’ demands for a national framework.

Ross Greer, co-leader of the Scottish Greens, who was outside Holyrood with protesters, said: “If we want to have the internet, we need datacentres and Scotland already has plenty of them.

“But some of these new hyper-scale datacentres of 120MW to 200MW – in total, those proposed would require more energy than all of Scotland needs at its peak at the moment. That is clearly not possible.”

The Scottish government has said that all planning authorities must notify ministers of new datacentre applications exceeding 50MW within a week to help monitor their impact on infrastructure, but underscored that the centres are important for economic growth.

The public finance minister for Scotland, Hannah Mary Goodlad, said: “We must balance the economic and employment interests in developing datacentres with national energy, climate and community wealth building ambitions, which are vital to our future prosperity, as well as the potential impact on local communities.

“I am clear that voices of communities that will be affected will be central to any considerations on datacentres.”

But Jones and the campaign want more. She fears that Scotland could be overwhelmed without a formal national strategy. “We are not saying everything needs to stop for ever. But it’s moving so fast. We need a pause.”
